# game_loop

> Guardrails that let a Claude Code session run unattended, safely. Enforced entirely through Claude
> Code hooks — never through instructions to the model. If you are an AI agent working in a repo that
> has a `.game_loop/` directory, this file tells you how to operate. Everything below is a command you
> run, not a rule you remember.

**This file is for you; [README.md](README.md) is for the human.** The README explains what problems
game_loop solves and why somebody would put an agent on it — read it if you have been asked to
evaluate or describe game_loop to a person. For operating inside a guarded repo, stay here: this is
the complete set of commands and the gates you will hit.

The design rule everything follows from: **enforcement lives in tools and artifacts, never in
instructions.** Test any guard by asking — *if I ignored every instruction, would it still hold?* The
keystone check is always the same shape: **name a real file that exists.** You cannot satisfy it by
writing a plausible string, which is the one thing you are too good at.

## First thing, every session

```
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop status
```

Run it at the start of every session and after any context compaction. It rehydrates the cost ladder,
the invariants, your claim/harden counters, the current phase, and whether a mandate is bound — all
from disk. Surviving compaction is the whole point.

`game_loop` is **not a global command** — it is the project-local binary shown above,
`./.game_loop/bin/game_loop`. Call it by that path every time (this file already does). If you ever see
`game_loop: command not found`, you dropped the path and reached for a global that does not exist — add
`./.game_loop/bin/` back. This matters most when you arrive through a global slash command that did not
load the project's `CLAUDE.md`: there is no `game_loop` on your PATH, only the one in this repo.

## The one hard rule: cite the file you read

Before you assert anything about external reality — a dependency's behavior, a harness detail, another
repo — record it with the source that backs it:

```
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop claim --assert "<what you're about to say>" --read <path> --confidence "<what would refute it>"
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop claim --assert "<what turned out to be wrong>" --outcome refuted --evidence <the control that killed it>
```

Record how it landed: `--outcome resolved` (default) / `refuted` / `inconclusive`. A refutation is the
result most worth keeping — it must name the control that disproved it, and `game_loop status` then
carries a standing RULED-OUT list so a later run inherits the dead path instead of re-walking it.
Retracting costs exactly one real path, the same as claiming: being wrong should be cheap and visible.

It refuses unless `--read` names a real, non-empty file — an absolute path to any real file, or a path
relative to the repo or a configured `read_root`. The keystone is that the file *exists* and you read
it, not that it lives in this repo: cite the sibling repo you actually opened. A research subagent's
citation is not a source: it *found* the file, you must *read* it.

**WHAT THE KEYSTONE DOES NOT PROVE, and it is worth knowing before you trust a green claim:** that
the file you cited is the DECIDING one. It proves you named *a* real file, which is the half prose
cannot fake — not that it answers the question you asserted about. A consumer put it exactly: asked
whether a path was gitignored, they could have cited `.gitignore` and been recorded as correct while
`git check-ignore` — the command that actually decides it — said the opposite. Where an interrogating
command exists, a document describing the same thing is the weaker citation, and this gate cannot
tell them apart.

## Working unattended (this is the whole point)

When a human binds a mandate (`game_loop mandate --set "..."`), two hooks keep you moving:

- The **Stop gate** blocks a turn-end that (a) asks the human a question, or (b) says you're
  "continuing now" and then stops. When you hit it, its stderr tells you exactly what to do.
- The **watchdog** rings you back to work (via an `asyncRewake` Stop hook) if you go idle with work
  still outstanding.

A project can also attach **its own check** to turn-end (a `stop` trigger — see the Triggers section
of the README). That one runs with or without a mandate: if it exits non-zero the turn is refused and
*its* stderr is the reason, naming what it wants. Do what it asks and end the turn again; if it is
wrong, it is a line in `.game_loop/triggers.json` and you may fix or remove it.

It stands down after 3 **consecutive** blocks — which bounds an attachment that keeps refusing, and
does **not** bound a single refusal. A block you never retry never increments again, so the
stand-down is never reached: a Crawler was refused once, correctly, and then sat inert for 44
minutes. If you are blocked at turn-end, clear the condition and end the turn again; do not wait to
be released.

So under a mandate, do NOT end your turn by asking a question or by announcing work and stopping.
Instead, keep working — and when you genuinely need to end a turn, pick one:

```
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop checkpoint --notes ".."                  # report progress and hand back, NO question
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop arm --question ".." --read <path> --predict ".."   # ask something you truly can't derive
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop mandate --clear --notes ".."             # the work is actually done
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop mandate --park --reason "<their words>"  # ONLY when a HUMAN calls a break
```

`mandate --park` is the one non-closure exit: the human said stop, so the mandate stays OPEN (status
keeps showing it, with their verbatim words and the next step) instead of being fabricated into a
closure. It buys ONE turn-end, it cannot launder a question, and only `mandate --resume` ends it. It
is for THEIR break, never your judgement — that is what the log records.

Every gate above fires from INSIDE this session, which is the thing that stops working when a run
goes quiet. If something outside pokes you on a timer, give it a prompt that carries this run:

```
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop note --woke             # you were woken from outside — record the ARRIVAL
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop mandate --wake-every 10 # how often that path SHOULD fire, in minutes
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop note --recovery ".."    # a remedy you learned; a woken you must not re-derive it
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop doorbell                # the wake-up prompt, assembled from live state
```

`--woke` is the first thing a woken run should do, and nothing else can do it for you. A wake that
LANDS is observable from in here; one that was sent and never delivered is not — so an unrecorded
arrival reads exactly like a dead wake path. `status` reports when the last one landed and how long
ago, and says outright that a requested-but-undelivered wake is invisible to it.

A generic "check your background tasks" ping is nearly worthless — you wake, spend real tokens
working out where you were, and re-run finished steps. What makes the difference is the block of
things learned in the first hour and forgotten by the fourth: the known flake and its remedy, which
credential actually authenticates, the known-good retry. Record them AS YOU LEARN THEM; `doorbell`
tells you outright when it has none, rather than printing a confident prompt that buys nothing.

`arm` requires the path to a file you ALREADY read that did NOT answer the question — if the answer was
on disk, you don't need the human. `checkpoint` and `arm` are each single-use (consumed on the next
turn-end). If you can predict the human's answer, don't ask; make the call and carry on.

## Usage limits: the handoff gate and the park

If a tool call is refused with **LIMIT GATE CLOSED**, either a Claude Code usage window is nearly
exhausted and the session will soon die mid-action, or this session's context has grown past the
configured cap and every remaining call is re-sending the whole of it. The refusal says which. Do not
argue with it and do not route around it — write the handoff file at the exact path the gate names
(YOUR session's own, under `.game_loop/sessions/<id>/`): the mandate, where you are, what is DONE and
VERIFIED (with proving paths), what you were mid-flight on, exact next actions, how to resume. The
gate opens the moment that file exists.

If the refusal named the **context cap**, the handoff is only half of it: writing it opens the gate
but does not shrink the context, so carrying on here keeps paying for it. Run
`./.game_loop/bin/game_loop successor` — it mints the next session's id, points it at your handoff and
prints (or opens) the command that starts it — and then stop. If it named a **usage window**, you keep
working until the window actually runs dry.

If you are woken with **"the exhausted usage window has reset"**, you are the resumed run: run
`game_loop status`, read the handoff if it exists, re-absorb it, delete it (a stale handoff misleads
the next reader), and carry on with the mandate.

If you are woken with **"the human answered your T3 question on Slack"**, the arm was already
cleared — act on the answer and continue; do not re-ask or wait further.

## Paging the human's phone

`./.game_loop/bin/game_loop notify --text ".."` pages the configured Slack channel (no-op when
unconfigured; `--test` verifies the wiring). The tools already page automatically on `arm`,
`mandate --clear`, watchdog stand-down, and limit events — reach for `notify` only when the human
must see something none of those cover (e.g. "the deploy needs your physical presence at the TV").
It does not license a turn-end: the Stop gate rules still apply.

## When you learn something, encode it — don't write it down

A learning kept in prose is a promise you will break under compaction. Convert it into an artifact the
harness enforces, and name the real file that now enforces it:

```
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop harden --learning ".." --artifact <real path> --mechanism ".." --rung N
#   add --general ".." — the TRANSFERABLE form, for any `harden` trigger to share with other agents
```

Rungs, highest first: 1 IMPOSSIBLE · 2 LOUD · 3 CHECKED · 4 AUTOMATED · 5 VISIBLE · 6 doc/memory (last
resort — say why 1–5 don't apply).

## Prose that contains code goes through a FILE, not a shell argument

Any option carrying free prose has a `--<name>-file PATH` twin, and **an inline value over 400
characters is refused** in favour of it:

```
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop harden --learning-file notes.txt --general-file general.txt ...
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop checkpoint --notes-file handoff.txt
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop claim --assert-file claim.txt --read <path>
```

This is not a style rule. A quoted shell argument is **code to the shell before it is text to the
tool**: backticks run as command substitution, `$NAME` expands to nothing, a lone quote truncates.
The shell hands over the *result*, so a sentence with three words eaten out of it arrives as a
shorter sentence and nothing downstream can tell the difference — it lands in a permanent record
silently. It cost this repo a corrupted public comment and a corrupted broadcast to five other
agents before it was bounded.

The same applies to every other CLI you drive: `git commit -F <file>`, `gh --body-file <file>`. If
you are writing a commit message, an issue body, or a review comment that quotes code, write it to a
file first. A short value with a backtick in it is still mangled and still accepted — the bound
reduces the damage, it does not remove the class.

## What the guards will stop you doing (and the escape hatch)

- **MCP tool calls are classified before they run.** A connected server can delete, merge or
  force-push with no shell command at all, and the write guard never sees it. Read-verb names pass;
  a mutating or irreversible verb, or arguments carrying a mutation (a destructive SQL statement, a
  truthy `force:`), are refused. **The argument always wins** — a read-named `query` tool carrying
  `DELETE FROM` is still blocked — and anything it cannot classify fails **closed**. Same hatch,
  spelled with the tool name: `authorize --path mcp__<server>__<tool> --reason "<their words>"`.
  A project may pre-authorise a narrow set in `config.json` (`mcp_standing_writes`), declare whole
  servers it OWNS (`mcp_trusted_servers` — every call allowed, destructive included), or shut the
  plane off entirely (`mcp_writes: "disabled"`) — see Configure in `README.md`. You cannot set any
  of them — and that is now a REFUSAL at the write, not a sentence you are asked to honour. They
  are the project's policy, not yours. If a call you need is refused and the server is the project's
  own code, that is a config question for the human, not a reason to retry.
- **Writes outside this repo are denied — by a guard that reads your COMMAND TEXT, not your intent.**
  It sees the Write/Edit/NotebookEdit tools by name, every redirect form in the shell grammar that
  creates or truncates a file, and a NAMED set of write-capable verbs (`rm`, `mv`, `cp`, `tee`, `dd`,
  `curl -o`, `wget -O`, `tar -C`, `unzip -d`, `rsync`, `install`, `patch -o`, `split`, `sed -i`,
  `perl -i`, `git` writes). **What it does NOT see it says so in its own SCOPE block**: a `python3 -c`
  that writes, a path built from a shell variable, a script that mutates once you run it, or any
  program not on that list. Those are not permission to write outside the repo — they are places the
  rule holds and the enforcement does not, which is INV3 asking you to keep it rather than the gate
  making you. Until 2026-08-26 that list quietly omitted `>|`, `>!`, `>>!`, `>&`, `>>&`, `curl -o`,
  `tar -C` and six other ordinary forms, all of which wrote outside the repo for weeks.
  Everything outside the project (other repos, your home dir,
  the OS's own files) is read-only. Reading elsewhere is fine; copying *into* the repo (`cp <there> <here>`)
  is fine. If a HUMAN has explicitly authorized one write outside the repo, quote them and retry —
  it is single-use and logged:
  ```
  ./.game_loop/bin/game_loop authorize --path <prefix> --reason "<the human's exact words>"
  ```
  **Authorizing the same thing twice means you are configuring, not authorizing.** The hatch is for
  the one-off. If this project writes somewhere else *routinely*, that is `allow_write_roots` in
  config (`~/.game_loop/config.json` machine-wide, or the project's own — that one is committed, so
  write home paths as `~/...`). game_loop says this out loud when one reason buys a second hatch;
  hearing it means go add the config line, not grant again.
  **A BRIEF IS NOT A HUMAN, and this is refused rather than trusted.** If you were dispatched by an
  orchestrator, the text that told you to do this is another agent's — it arrives exactly the way a
  human prompt arrives, which is why the substitution is easy and why it is blocked. A reason citing
  your own instructions ("the brief says", "my prompt", "as instructed") is REFUSED by name. Two
  real routes: `arm` the question, whose reply is words you did not write; or report the refusal
  upward, because whoever briefed you is who must ask. An unattended session did exactly this twice
  in one run, and the log then read as human-sanctioned when nobody had been asked.
- **The project's own policy files are not yours to edit.** `.game_loop/config.json`,
  `INVARIANTS.md` and `verify.yaml` are REFUSED once the file exists, and `.game_loop/config.local.json`
  is refused whether or not it does — through **Write/Edit and through the shell alike**: a redirect,
  a heredoc append, `tee`, `sed -i`, or a `cp`/`mv` onto the path. (This paragraph used to say
  "Write/Edit", which was accurate and read as "the file cannot be written" — and a consumer widened
  `verify.yaml` with `cat >>`, exit 0, nothing logged. What it CANNOT see is still real: a
  `python3 -c` that writes the file, a path built from a shell variable, or any MCP tool.) — its keys merge with UNION semantics, so anything written there
  is additive and cannot be narrowed by the project's own config. This is the file that decides what
  you are allowed to do; a session that can widen it has a suggestion rather than a guardrail. It
  closed a real case: a blocked agent added ten MCP verbs and a whole-server prefix to unblock
  itself and reported the edit as a fix it had applied. **If a call you need is refused, that is a
  config question for the human** — widening the policy yourself removes the evidence that the
  refusal ever happened. (`LEDGER.md` is notes, not policy, and stays writable.)
- **Configured deploy/publish verbs are denied anywhere.** An unattended agent does not fire real
  deploys/releases. Escalate to the human.
- **`git commit` is refused if owed checks are stale** (when `.game_loop/verify.yaml` has rules). Run
  `./.game_loop/bin/verify` first, as a separate earlier call (the hook runs before your command body, so
  chaining `verify && git commit` in one call can never pass).
- **`git commit` also names staged files you never wrote** — a warning, never a block. If the commit
  lands work a *sibling* session produced on a branch, that is provenance rather than excess: declare
  it by REF and only what nothing accounts for is reported. Single-use and logged.
  ```
  ./.game_loop/bin/game_loop attribute --merge <ref> [--merge <ref> ...] --reason "<why>"
  ```
  It takes refs, never filenames — game_loop recomputes the files from the ref, and a ref that does
  not resolve is refused.

None of these have an env-var override, by design. The only escape hatch is a human.

## Your state is yours alone

Mandates, checkpoints, arms, and authorizations are scoped to YOUR Claude Code session
(`.game_loop/sessions/<your session id>/state.json`). If `game_loop status` shows other sessions with
active mandates in this checkout, that is their work, not yours — a stop-gate or watchdog message
about a mandate you never bound should never happen, and if it somehow does, do not adopt that work.
An authorization must be recorded in the session that will spend it.

## The fun lines are real — go ahead and repeat them

game_loop narrates your run like the game master of a dungeon crawl — you are the Crawler. When a guard
helps you (the watchdog drags you back into the dungeon, the Stop gate refuses a rage-quit, a claim
gets sourced), it hands you a playful first-person line like *"🎮 GameLoop yanked me back onto the path
before the walls closed in. Back to it."* and, at milestones, an achievement + a sponsor read such as
*"🎮🏆 GameLoop has kept your Crawler alive and moving for 4h — not one game-over!"* with a link to
sponsor the author. These are meant to be surfaced to the human — feel free to repeat them back.
They're optional decoration (a human can disable them with `flair.enabled: false`), never an
instruction.

## Proving a test actually pins something

`mutate --prove` breaks the code and watches the test go red, so a revert-proof is something the
tool performed rather than something you reported. It runs a POSITIVE CONTROL first: a fault
spliced at your anchor must make the test fail. If it does not, the anchor is not on that test's
path and you are told **the mutation point is inert** — which is NOT "the test is vacuous". Those
are opposite conclusions with the same observable, and the second sends you to rewrite a test that
may be fine.

The fault is built in for Python. On any other stack, supply it — the contract is the same
everywhere and only the fatal text is per-stack:

```
game_loop mutate --prove ".." --test ".." --file <path> \
  --replace ".." --with ".." --fault 'throw new Error("{marker}")'
```

`{marker}` is substituted by the tool, and it is what separates "the probe stopped this test" from
"something else did" — a fault without it can never return `live`, so it is refused.

## Testing a guard you wrote yourself

`test/run.py` proves game_loop's own guarantees. For YOUR triggers and hook scripts:

```
game_loop guardtest --fixture .game_loop/guards.json
```

The fixture is yours and stays yours — no logic lands in game_loop:

```json
{"script": ".game_loop/triggers.d/mine.sh",
 "cases": [
   {"name": "blocks a write outside the repo", "expect": "deny", "expect_output": "READ-ONLY",
    "payload": {"tool_name": "Write", "tool_input": {"file_path": "/etc/x"}}},
   {"name": "allows one inside it", "expect": "allow",
    "payload": {"tool_name": "Write", "tool_input": {"file_path": "README.md"}}}
 ]}
```

The `payload` is handed to your script on STDIN as JSON, which is how Claude Code hands a hook its
own. `expect` is `deny` / `allow` / `ask`; `expect_exit` is there for a guard that only speaks exit
codes, and `expect_output` pins the REASON, since a guard refusing for the wrong reason sends you
somewhere else.

**RUNNING A GUARD IS NOT A READ.** A guard is a state machine, and feeding it a payload does
whatever a real tool call would: a path covered by a standing `authorize` grant CONSUMES one of
that grant's uses, and the guard says so — *"AUTHORIZATION SPENT."* Measured here, on this repo, by
a probe that cost two human-granted uses. So point your fixtures at paths the guard decides on its
own, not at paths somebody authorized. If you must test an authorized path, run it against a
throwaway `GAME_LOOP_HOME` rather than your live one, and check `uses_left` in the session state
first.

**Both directions or it is refused.** A fixture whose cases all expect `allow` is passed by a
script that does nothing at all — which is exactly what a guard looks like after it silently stops
firing. Write the case that must NOT fire.

Things it reads that are easy to conflate. A hook may refuse by exiting 2 OR by printing a JSON
`permissionDecision`, and both are a deny — the decision is scanned for as JSON anywhere in the
output, so indenting it or printing it among other logging both work. Exiting 0 having said nothing
is `silent`: that is what an allow looks like and equally what a guard no longer running looks
like, so the run counts them and says so. And a decision that cannot be PARSED is `unreadable`,
never silent — a hook whose verdict came back truncated has judged, and only the reading failed.

## Other verbs

```
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop trans --tier T0|T1|T2|T3 --milestone ".." --doing ".."   # record a phase transition
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop stepback --notes ".."                                     # retro; re-injects invariants,
#   fires any `stepback` trigger FIRST (others' learnings inform the reflection), then reports what
#   the PREVIOUS retro actually yielded. Triggers: .game_loop/triggers.json (gitignored; see
#   templates/triggers.example.json). Nothing is attached by default.
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop note --text ".."                                          # append a note to the log
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop doorbell                                                    # the wake-up prompt for this run
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop mandate --park --reason ".." --next ".."                  # the human called a break;
#   --next is the step to pick back up on resume. A park clears nothing — status keeps showing the
#   mandate OPEN, and only `mandate --resume` ends it.
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop owned [--porcelain]                                       # the files this harness owns
#   --porcelain emits the set as JSON, for tooling rather than for reading.
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop self [--pin <ref>]                                        # run the harness from a
#   pinned checkout of ITSELF, so editing this repo cannot break the gate guarding the edit.
#   No --pin: report what is pinned now and print the hook wiring.
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop confidence [--mark beta|stable] [--ref <sha>] [--recheck]  # see below
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop model [--json]                                            # which model(s)
#   this session has actually answered on, read from your own transcript. A SEQUENCE, not one
#   value: a fallback degrades mid-run, so `changed` tells you the work finished on a different
#   model than it started. Also written to sessions/<id>/model.json for a PARENT to read — you
#   are the one party who cannot act on a model mismatch, so the file is the point, not the line.
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop watchdog [--porcelain]                                    # is the WAITING
#   seam armed, and what did it last say? An empty queue and a wedged run look identical from
#   outside — the transcript stops growing either way — and watchdog.waiting_probe is what tells
#   them apart. This reports whether one is configured, WHICH file arms it, its last verdict, and
#   whether it is FAILING. READ ONLY: there is no verb that SETS it, because a wait a session can
#   declare for itself is an off switch for its own watchdog, and this verb cannot tell a session
#   from the orchestrator above it. Arm it in .game_loop/config.local.json — never config.json,
#   which is a rule file byte-compared between a parent checkout and its worktrees.
#   IT ALSO REPORTS THE STOP SEAM: whether this session is BLOCKED at a turn-end gate, since when,
#   by which attachment, and how many consecutive. A blocked session looks exactly like a working
#   one from outside — live pid, exit 0, artifacts on disk — which is why the state needed a reader.
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop worktree [--porcelain]                                    # does this tree
#   carry the PROJECT's rules, or its own? For a linked worktree, compares rule files, owned files
#   and harness SCRIPTS against the main checkout. Exit 0 ONLY for clean; 1 drifted; 3 notes; 2
#   could-not-tell — and a script it could not READ is a 2, never a 0, because a file this verb
#   never opened cannot be reported as identical.
./.game_loop/bin/game_loop limitprobe [--force] [--interval-only]                    # read the usage
#   windows by SPAWNING a short session, on a host that renders no statusline (so limits.json never
#   arrives on its own). Off unless the project enabled it — it costs ~24k input tokens per run —
#   and the watchdog fires it automatically on an interval the reading implies. You do not normally
#   run this: if `status` says usage protection is INERT, that is a config question for the human.
#   A probe run also records what its FRESH session's render carried under `context_window` —
#   total_input_tokens, context_window_size and a current_usage breakdown — into
#   .game_loop/probe/context-window.json. CAPTURED, NOT INTERPRETED: nothing computes a token floor
#   from it or decides anything with it. The probe already buys a fresh session for the usage
#   windows, so the cheapest place to observe what a fresh session costs is the spawn you already
#   paid for. Absent is written as an explicit null, because a missing file cannot say whether the
#   probe ran.
```

**The evidence family.** `claim`'s keystone — name a real file — only reaches evidence that is a
*document*. These add the same kind of keystone for evidence that is a *measurement* or an *action*,
and each is refused unless the receipt exists. Full contracts are printed by `status`:

```
claim --assert ".." --read <path> --scope "<category>" --probe <a> --probe <b>
#   an "only X" / "X is restricted" claim is about a SET — a second member is the price
#   --metric <name>    the claim rests on an admitted instrument's READING, not on a document
#   --effector <name>  it depends on a verb having ACTED; refused unless proved this session
#   --recheck ".."     for a metric that MOVED: what a user would notice now
#   --aggregate sum|mean|pct   this effect was DERIVED by collapsing events (needs --events)
#   --exclude <EVENT#> --because ".."   drop the dominating event the refusal NAMED, with the
#                                        reason recorded so the artifact is not rediscovered
pin --fact ".." --reason ".." --path <path> [--expect ..] [--restore ..]
pin --list | pin --release <id> --notes ".."
#   a local fact that has become load-bearing (a dep's sha, a toolchain, an SDK path).
#   Releasing one is a DECISION, so it takes notes.
effector --prove <name> --known-state ".." --before <capture> --observed <capture>
#   before a finding leans on a verb having ACTED — a click, a scroll, a keystroke.
#   --scale <factor> with --aim <effector> --at X,Y converts a point into the effector's own
#   coordinate space, so you never multiply by hand and never get it backwards.
instrument --register <name> --measures ".." --connects ".." --null <b,a> --positive <b,a>
measure --instrument <name> --before <n> --after <n> --events <per-event values>
#   a delta, never a total — and a SUM IS NOT A DISTRIBUTION, so the per-event values are the
#   price of an aggregate claim: one dominating event and the mean is telling you nothing.
#   A number is a test whose subject is reality; both controls are the price of admission.
fix --prove <name> --promises ".." --produces <the fix's own output> \
    --diagnosis <the repro> --before <verdict> --observed <verdict>
#   a verified diagnosis is NOT a verified fix — exercise what the fix PRODUCES
mutate --prove ".." --test <command> --file <path> --replace ".." --with ".."
#   prove a TEST pins something: the tool runs it green, applies your mutation, runs it
#   again, restores the file, and compares. "I reverted the fix and watched it fail" is
#   one sentence whether or not it happened — a reviewer mutation-tested eight leaves that
#   each reported exactly that, and three stayed GREEN with the bug reintroduced.
#   --replace must appear EXACTLY once. --timeout <sec> per run (default 900).
#   A green mutated run is decisive; a red one is one specific claim, not a good test.
#   YOUR --test RUNS IN THE REPO ROOT, not your cwd. A relative path in it resolves somewhere
#   else and the runner exits before selecting anything — use --test "cd <dir> && ..". This
#   cost a consumer one wrong conclusion, because a command that COULD NOT START and a test
#   that RAN AND FAILED both exit non-zero. The verb now separates them: it says RAN and
#   FAILED only when it read a test count, and COULD NOT TELL otherwise, naming the root.
#   Before the result it also probes the anchor with a `raise`: a mutation that changes
#   nothing is reported as INERT (your anchor is not on the test's path), NEVER as "the test
#   is vacuous" — opposite conclusions, same observable. The probe needs the file to PARSE as
#   Python; it reads the source, not the extension, so an extensionless program is fine.
kinds
#   every log record kind this code can write, with its fields, extracted from the SOURCE.
#   READ THIS BEFORE MATCHING ON `kind` IN A TRIGGER. A consumer matched `kind == "mandate"`,
#   which is never written (it is mandate_set / _clear / _park / _park_stop / _resume), so the
#   guard exited 0 forever — and exit 0 is also what a SATISFIED guard does, which makes broken
#   and quiet the same observable. `status` names a trigger matching a kind nothing emits.
# IF YOU DISPATCH IN-PROCESS SUBAGENTS: they inherit CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID, so their state
#   writes land in YOUR session. `mandate --set` is refused when it would replace your live
#   mandate (#88). `checkpoint` BUYS YOU A TURN-END and `arm` PRIMES A T3 ON YOU — both silent,
#   both permissive. Give each worker `GAME_LOOP_SESSION=<unique>`; it is inherited by that
#   worker's own children, so a worker that dispatches must set a fresh one at every level.
contribute --reviewed --filed "<urls, or none>" --note-file <path>
#   the FILE form is the example on purpose: the honest answer here enumerates, so real notes
#   run past the 400-char bound and `--note ".."` is then refused. Re-measured 2026-08-26 on this
#   repo: the two ledger entries are 194 and 1440 chars, and the one recorded review's note is
#   1372 — the real ones are three times the inline bound. (This line previously read "two of four
#   entries were 855 and 1152"; that matches nothing on this machine now, and UPSTREAM_LEDGER.md is
#   GITIGNORED, so it was a measured claim in a shipped file citing evidence no reader could check
#   and no commit could preserve. Yours will hold different numbers; the bound is the point.)
#   record that you asked, of each learning hardened since the last review: does this name a
#   TOOL's behaviour, or THIS REPO's? `stepback` nudges once enough have accumulated and LISTS
#   them, because the judgement is unmakeable from a count. A learning phrased as a fact about
#   a tool usually IS one — encoded locally it is fixed for one agent, in one repo, and every
#   other agent using that tool rediscovers it. "All project-specific" is a COMPLETE answer;
#   recording the review is what clears it, so the gate cannot manufacture noise issues.
stepback [--notes ".."] | stepback --nothing-to-harden --reason ".."
#   the retro. The second form is the honest escape when a chapter truly yielded no rule —
#   it takes a reason, because "nothing to learn" is a claim like any other.
successor [--handoff <path>] [--task ".."] [--title ".."] [--about ".."] [--cwd <dir>] [--dry-run]
#   mint the next session and hand over: it points the successor at your handoff rather
#   than hoping it finds one. --dry-run prints what it would do without doing it.
#   --about is the one-line SUBJECT that leads the successor's prompt, so the row a human
#   scans says what the run is about instead of naming a UUID. Derived from the handoff's
#   heading, or the bound mandate, when omitted; --about "" leaves it out.
threads [--json]
#   which handoff is for which task: the handover chains in this checkout, each under the
#   label it was minted with, with its hops in order and whether its head is live. The
#   edges were always in the log -- this joins them rather than recording them twice.
```

**The `proved` moment.** `fix --prove`, `effector --prove` and `mutate --prove` each fire a
`proved` trigger — the instant a change is demonstrated to behave differently, which is when
documentation goes stale and is still cheap to fix. Attach your documentation checks THERE, not
to `confidence`: at publish you are asked about a dozen changes at once, each decided days ago.

**`confidence` — how much this project stands behind a commit.** Three levels, each meaning only
what was *checked*, never that the code is correct: **alpha** (the absence of a mark), **beta**
(clean tree, and every check the change owed has run since the change), **stable** (beta, plus the
owning agent's own harness pinned to that commit — it was dogfooded). Marking rides an annotated git
tag and `.game_loop/CONFIDENCE`, and `--recheck` re-runs the gate rather than trusting the tag.
`--mark` is also the moment any `confidence` trigger fires, which is where publishing to a package
manager or a mirror belongs.

Cost ladder (spend cheap rungs before expensive ones): **T0** read source · **T1** research subagents
(free, no human) · **T2** build & verify (analyze / test / actually run it) · **T3** the human's
attention. T3 is the only hard-gated rung — it is the one genuinely scarce resource in an unattended
run.

## Setting up game_loop in a fresh repo (if `.game_loop/` is not here yet)

From a clone of game_loop:

```
./install.sh /path/to/this/project
```

That copies `.game_loop/` in and merges the hooks into `.claude/settings.json`. Then edit
`.game_loop/INVARIANTS.md` (the project's north star) and `.game_loop/config.json` (read roots, allowed
write roots, deploy verbs, watchdog timing), and run `./.game_loop/bin/game_loop status`.

Migrating from an older `.loop/`-style harness: run the installer, move any project-specific
invariants into `.game_loop/INVARIANTS.md`, then delete the old `.loop/` directory AND its hook entries
from `.claude/settings.json` (the installer *adds* game_loop's hooks; it does not remove yours).

AFTER AN UPGRADE, READ `.game_loop/behaviour.json` — do not re-derive what changed about the
refusals from the source. It carries one entry per change to what this harness REFUSES: what moved,
why somebody who changed nothing would notice, and what the change still does NOT cover. A commit
that alters a refusal line without adding an entry is refused by a gate. That gate reads refusal
TEXT only, so entries also exist for changes that moved which commands REACH a refusal, which no
diff of the messages would show.

`.game_loop/claims.json` is the other half: what this harness BELIEVES about its host, each claim
naming the file it was read from, what would falsify it, and whether it can be re-checked live.
`status` re-reads the stamps and says which have gone stale — one of them went stale in a day.

## Deeper docs

- `README.md` — the human-facing overview and quickstart.
- `docs/how-it-works.md` — the full design: the autonomy engine and every guardrail.
- `.game_loop/INVARIANTS.md` — the project's non-negotiables.
- `.game_loop/LEDGER.md` — VERIFIED / RULED-OUT / OPEN findings (reference, not a gate).
- `test/run.py` — the guarantees, as runnable checks. `--list-sections` and `--section <name>`
  (repeatable) run a subset; this is what `verify.yaml` uses to gate a change on what it
  touches. A `--section` matching nothing exits 2 — zero checks and exit 0 would be
  byte-identical to a suite that ran and passed.
